name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1
evidenceNote: Its activity is described in cell studies, supplier data, and patents. The only published human study found tests a serum mixing it with other peptides, so no result can be credited to this ingredient alone.
summary: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a fatty-acid-linked GHK peptide used in anti-wrinkle creams such as the Matrixyl 3000 blend. Human evidence for it alone is lacking.
keyTakeaway: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is the three-amino-acid peptide GHK (glycine, histidine, lysine) with a palmitic acid tail attached to help it enter skin. It is a cosmetic ingredient made by Sederma, sold alone and as half of the Matrixyl 3000 blend with palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7. Cell studies suggest it prompts skin fibroblasts to make collagen and other support proteins. Human evidence is thin: one 32-person, 28-day study of a multi-peptide eye serum reported fewer wrinkles, but had no placebo and could not isolate this ingredient. As a cosmetic it needs no FDA approval, provided labels stick to appearance claims.

blocks.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a lab-made cosmetic ingredient. Its core is GHK, a three-amino-acid sequence (glycine, histidine, lysine) found in collagen, joined to palmitic acid, a common fatty acid [2]. The fat tail makes the peptide more oily, which is meant to help it cross the outer layer of skin. In ingredient lists it is sometimes written as pal-GHK.

For about two decades it was sold under the name palmitoyl oligopeptide, a label that confusingly covered two different molecules. In 2013 the name was retired and the two were given distinct names, one of which is palmitoyl tripeptide-1 [2]. The supplier, Sederma (part of Croda), sells it on its own as Biopeptide CL and combined with palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 as Matrixyl 3000, a common anti-aging peptide blend [3].

It is classed as a signal peptide, meaning it is meant to send a message to skin cells rather than fill or plump the skin directly. In cell culture, it is reported to act through the TGF-beta pathway and push dermal fibroblasts, the cells that build skin's support layer, to make more extracellular matrix proteins such as collagen [3]. The idea is that short collagen fragments are a natural cue that matrix has been broken down and needs rebuilding.

Whether enough of it reaches those cells in real skin is an open question. A review of anti-wrinkle peptides concluded that most have poor skin permeability, because peptides tend to be large, water-loving, and easily broken down by skin enzymes, and that many may not reach their targets at useful concentrations without delivery aids [5]. The palmitic acid tail is one such aid, but how well it works for this peptide in finished products has not been measured independently.

No, and as a cosmetic ingredient it does not need to be. Under US law, cosmetics and their ingredients (apart from color additives) can be sold without FDA approval [1]. What decides whether a product is a cosmetic or a drug is its intended use, judged largely by the claims made for it. A cream that promises to improve the look of fine lines stays a cosmetic. A product claiming to regenerate cells or treat a disease is making drug claims and would need drug approval [1].
That is why products containing palmitoyl tripeptide-1 talk about firmer-looking skin and smoother appearance rather than rebuilding collagen inside the body.

Very little of the evidence is independent. A 2021 review of cosmetic peptides found that most information about palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and its relatives appears in patents and supplier brochures rather than peer-reviewed journals, and that randomized clinical studies are few [2]. One review repeats a report that Biopeptide CL performs comparably to retinoids without their irritation, but no published head-to-head trial backs that up [3].

blocks.text: The eye serum study is the closest thing to human data. It was a single-group study with instrument measurements and questionnaires, co-authored with a biotechnology company, and the serum contained palmitoyl tripeptide-1 together with palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 and other peptides [3][4]. With no comparison group and several actives, it cannot show what this ingredient contributes. Settling the question would take a randomized, vehicle-controlled trial of palmitoyl tripeptide-1 on its own, measured over months rather than weeks, and no such trial has been published.

Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is used in leave-on creams and serums, and none of the studies cited here reported safety problems with it. In the eye serum study, no product-related adverse reactions were seen [4]. A review of peptides in sensitive-skin products notes that their safety data come mainly from manufacturers and from the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel [2]. As with any skin product, irritation or allergy remains possible in individuals.
